title: JESUS KNEW LAZARUS WOULD LIVE AGAIN… SO WHY DID HE BREAK DOWN AND WEEP?
paragraphs: JESUS KNEW LAZARUS WOULD LIVE AGAIN… SO WHY DID HE BREAK DOWN AND WEEP?

He already knew the grave was about to surrender its prisoner. He already knew the miracle was coming. But standing before that tomb, the Son of God did something that should forever change how you understand your own suffering.
There is something about Jesus standing outside Lazarus' tomb that should stop every hurting Christian in their tracks.
Because Jesus knew.
He knew Lazarus was dead before He arrived in Bethany. He knew what He was about to do. He knew that within moments, a man who had been lying in a tomb for four days would walk out alive.
And yet…
Jesus wept.
Not because the situation had caught Him by surprise.
Not because death had defeated Him.
Not because He had suddenly discovered that the Father was powerless to help.
He wept while knowing that resurrection was coming.
Read that again, because somewhere in those few words is a truth that could change the way you see every tear you have ever cried.
Jesus knew how the story would end, but He still entered the sorrow of the people living through it.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to understand tonight.
You have been praying. Waiting. Trying to trust God while something in your life seems to be falling apart.
You know the Scriptures. You have heard the sermons. You believe God is sovereign.
But your heart still hurts.
And sometimes, in the silence between your prayers and God's answer, you wonder something you are almost afraid to say aloud.
"If God already knows what He is going to do… why does He let me cry like this?"
Come with me to Bethany.
Because the answer is not found in a cold explanation about suffering.
It is found in the tears of Jesus Christ.
And what happened outside that tomb is far more astonishing than many of us realize.
Lazarus was not a stranger to Jesus.
He was loved.
John 11:5 says plainly:
"Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus." (KJV)
That detail matters.
Because when Lazarus became seriously ill, his sisters did not send Jesus a complicated theological argument.
They sent a message that rested entirely on His love.
"Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." (John 11:3, KJV)
Notice what they did not say.
They did not remind Jesus how much Lazarus had done for Him.
They did not present a list of good works.
They did not claim that Lazarus deserved healing because he was faithful.
They simply appealed to the love of Christ.
The one You love is sick.

And if you have ever prayed for someone lying in a hospital bed, watched a loved one deteriorate, or begged God to intervene before something terrible happened, you can probably feel the desperation behind that message.
Jesus, please come.
We need You.
But then the story takes a turn that is almost unbearable.
John 11:6 says:
"When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was."
Two more days.
Jesus loved Lazarus.
Jesus knew Lazarus was sick.
And Jesus remained where He was.
That is the part of the story that can make a wounded believer uncomfortable.
Because we want love to mean immediate intervention.

We want God's affection to guarantee that the ambulance arrives in time, the marriage survives, the medical results come back clear, the child returns home, and the person we cannot imagine living without gets another year.
But John refuses to let us confuse Christ's love with our preferred timing.
Jesus loved them.
And He delayed.
Not because He was indifferent.
Not because He had forgotten.
And certainly not because He enjoyed their suffering.
Earlier, Jesus had explained that Lazarus' illness would become an occasion for the glory of God to be revealed through the Son (John 11:4).
There was a purpose the sisters could not yet see.
But be careful here.
This passage does not give us permission to tell every grieving person that their tragedy happened for the same reason Lazarus died.
It does not promise that every terminal illness will end in a miraculous recovery.
And it does not mean that God is pleased by human pain.
It reveals something specific about Jesus and this particular moment in redemptive history.
The love of Christ was present even when His timing was incomprehensible.
And that truth becomes painfully personal when Jesus finally arrives.
Lazarus has already been in the tomb for four days.
The mourners have gathered.
The burial has taken place.
The sisters have endured the kind of silence that makes a house feel unfamiliar.
And Martha goes out to meet Jesus.
Her first words are devastating.
"Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." (John 11:21, KJV)
Mary will later say essentially the same thing.
Can you hear what is underneath those words?
Lord, we called You.
Lord, we believed You could help.
Lord, we knew You loved him.
Where were You?
It is the cry of someone whose faith has not disappeared but whose heart has been shattered.
And there is something remarkable about how Jesus responds.
He does not shame Martha for bringing her grief into His presence.
He does not dismiss her pain with a religious slogan.
He leads her toward one of the greatest declarations ever spoken.
"I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." (John 11:25, KJV)
In the Greek text, Jesus says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.
"I am the resurrection and the life."
Not merely, "I can perform a resurrection."
Not simply, "I know something about life after death."
I AM the resurrection and the life.
Jesus is not presenting resurrection as a distant religious theory.
He is revealing that life itself is found in Him.
This is the center of the entire encounter.
Before Lazarus walks out of the tomb, Jesus calls Martha to believe in who He is.
And that matters because Christianity is not ultimately built upon the promise that every painful situation will be reversed before we die.
It is built upon Jesus Christ, who conquered death through His own death and resurrection.
The miracle at Bethany points beyond Bethany.
It points to the Savior who would soon enter His own tomb.
But we are not there yet.
Because before Jesus calls Lazarus out…
He sees Mary crying.
He sees the people who came with her weeping.
And something happens inside Him.
John 11:33 says that Jesus "groaned in the spirit, and was troubled."
The original Greek is particularly revealing.
The word translated "groaned" is ἐνεβριμήσατο (enebrimēsato), from the verb embrimaomai.
It can express a forceful inward reaction, including indignation or stern emotion.
This is not merely the language of quiet sadness.
John portrays Jesus as deeply and powerfully moved.

Scholars discuss precisely what provoked this response. Some emphasize indignation toward death and its devastation. Others also consider the surrounding unbelief, grief, and the circumstances of the scene.
The text does not explicitly identify one exclusive object of His indignation.
But it certainly does not portray Jesus as emotionally detached.
He is profoundly disturbed.
And then comes the shortest verse in many English Bibles.
"Jesus wept." (John 11:35, KJV)
Two words in English.
A world of meaning.
In Greek:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
"Jesus wept."
The verb dakryō describes shedding tears.
John uses a different Greek verb here from the one describing the mourning of Mary and those around her in the preceding verses.
That distinction should not be exaggerated into a claim that Jesus felt no real grief.
His tears were real.
His humanity was real.
His love was real.
And the people watching understood something important.
"Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!" (John 11:36, KJV)
They saw His tears and recognized His affection.
And now we reach the question that has troubled so many hearts.
Why would Jesus cry over a man He was about to raise?
Because knowing the victory does not make the suffering meaningless.
Because the certainty of resurrection does not make death a good thing.
Because love does not become emotionless simply because it knows the future.
And because Jesus Christ did not enter our broken world merely to demonstrate supernatural power from a comfortable distance.
He entered it as the Word made flesh.
John 1:14 tells us:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
Think about that.
The eternal Son of God took on genuine human nature.
He did not pretend to be human.
He did not borrow a human body while remaining untouched by human experience.
He became truly man without ceasing to be truly God.
And standing at Lazarus' tomb, the incarnate Son did not treat death like an insignificant inconvenience.
He confronted the devastation it had brought into the lives of people He loved.
That is why this moment matters so much.
The same Jesus who had power over the grave had tears for the grieving.
Some people have been taught, directly or indirectly, that strong faith means never crying.
That if you really trust God, you will always smile.
That sorrow is evidence of spiritual weakness.
But that teaching cannot survive John 11.
Jesus wept.
And Jesus was not lacking faith.
He was not doubting the Father.
He was not spiritually immature.
His tears were not a contradiction of His holiness.
They were an expression of His genuine humanity and love.
So please hear this.
The tears you shed at your father's funeral do not automatically mean you have forgotten the resurrection.
The ache you feel when you remember your mother does not mean your faith has failed.
The nights you cry over your marriage, your child, your loneliness, or the life you thought you would have are not, by themselves, evidence that God has abandoned you.
There is a difference between grieving and surrendering to unbelief.
There is a difference between asking God why and declaring that God cannot be trusted.
And there is a difference between tears that fall from a wounded heart and a heart that refuses to bring its wounds to Christ.
The Bible does not command Christians to become emotionally numb.
Paul tells believers not to grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
Notice carefully.
He does not say, "Do not grieve."
He teaches us to grieve differently.
With hope.
With the resurrection in view.
With confidence that death will not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus.
Christian hope does not erase grief. It changes what grief is allowed to tell us about the future.
And perhaps you have needed someone to say that for a very long time.
Perhaps you have been carrying guilt because you still cry about something that happened years ago.
Perhaps people told you to move on.
Perhaps they quoted Scripture without sitting long enough to hear your story.
Perhaps they made you feel that your pain was an inconvenience.
But look at Jesus.
He knows what He is about to do.
And still He weeps.
Not because He is powerless.
But because His power does not cancel His compassion.
That is a Savior worth knowing.
Yet there is another part of this account that we must not overlook.
Jesus does not remain outside the tomb crying.
He approaches it.
And when He arrives, He commands them to remove the stone.
Martha immediately protests.
"Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days." (John 11:39, KJV)
Four days.
This was not a misunderstanding about whether Lazarus was sleeping.
John emphasizes the reality of his death.
The situation was humanly irreversible.
And that is exactly where Jesus publicly reveals His authority.
After praying to the Father, He cries out with a loud voice:
"Lazarus, come forth." (John 11:43, KJV)
The Greek is strikingly direct:
Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω
Lazare, deuro exō.
"Lazarus, come out!"
No elaborate ritual.
No struggle against an equal opponent.
No uncertainty about whether His command would be obeyed.
The voice of Jesus enters a place where human voices can no longer summon a response.
And John tells us:
"And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes." (John 11:44, KJV)
Imagine being there.
One moment, the entrance to the tomb is dark.
The next, the man everyone buried is standing before them.
The sisters who had wept over his body now see him alive.
The mourners who had come to comfort them witness something beyond ordinary human explanation.
The man who had been dead for four days has returned.
But don't miss the most important detail.
Lazarus came out because Jesus called him.
The power was not in Lazarus' determination.
The power was not in the strength of his faith while he lay dead.
The power was in the Son of God.
And this miracle becomes a breathtaking picture of the spiritual life Christ gives.
Ephesians 2:1 describes humanity as dead in trespasses and sins.
Not merely confused.
Not simply in need of encouragement.
Spiritually dead.
Yet Ephesians 2:4–5 declares that God, rich in mercy and great in love, makes believers alive together with Christ.
Salvation is not the story of spiritually dead people making themselves alive through religious effort.
It is the story of divine grace reaching people who could never save themselves.
And this is where the story of Lazarus reaches beyond the cemetery.
Because perhaps your deepest problem is not the sorrow you have been carrying.
Perhaps it is the sin you have been hiding.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The secret addiction.
The dishonesty.
The pride.
The resentment you have justified for years.
The public appearance of Christianity while your private life is moving farther from Christ.
You know the right words.
You know how to worship when other people are watching.
You know how to post Bible verses.
But somewhere beneath the religious language, your conscience has been whispering that something is wrong.
And you have become very good at silencing it.
Friend, Jesus did not come merely to improve your reputation.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God through His death.
He came to call us to repentance and faith.
He came to forgive, cleanse, and transform.
And there is a difference between wanting Jesus to remove the consequences of sin and wanting Him to become Lord of your life.
One asks for relief.
The other bows in surrender.
The Gospel offers forgiveness freely through Christ, but the grace that saves us does not leave us comfortable in the sin from which He came to rescue us.
You cannot purchase this grace.
You cannot earn it through donations.
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." (Ephesians 2:8, KJV)
That is why the words From Scandal to Grace mean so much.
The scandal of our rebellion.
The shame we could never wash away by ourselves.
The guilt we tried to bury.
And then the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
Grace that does not deny our sin but deals with it through the cross.
Grace that does not pretend we were innocent but offers forgiveness through the One who was.
Grace that calls us out of darkness and into a new life of repentance, faith, and obedience.
Because Jesus does not merely rewrite how people see your story. He changes your standing before God.
And here is something else about Lazarus that we must remember.
Lazarus was raised, but his return to earthly life was not the final resurrection promised to God's people.
He would still live in a mortal body.
The miracle was a sign pointing to something greater.
Jesus Himself would soon die.
The religious authorities would intensify their plans against Him following the events at Bethany (John 11:45–53).
The One who called Lazarus out of the grave would go willingly toward the cross.
He would bear the sins of His people.
He would be buried.
And on the third day, He would rise, never to die again.
Romans 6:9 declares:
"Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him."
There is the greater victory.
Lazarus was restored to mortal life.
Jesus rose in resurrection glory.
Lazarus' tomb was a sign.
Christ's empty tomb is central to the Gospel itself.
And that changes how we understand His tears.
The One who wept over death would go on to defeat death.
The One who stood beside a grieving family would accomplish the redemption that gives believers eternal hope.
The One who loved Lazarus would demonstrate the immeasurable depth of divine love through His own sacrifice.
So when you ask why Jesus wept, remember this.
He was not crying because resurrection was impossible.
He was weeping in the presence of a real enemy whose devastation He had come to overcome.
And in His compassion, we glimpse the heart of the Savior.
But there is a painful truth we must face.
Not every tomb opens when we ask.
Not every person we pray for recovers.
Not every family gets the miracle it desperately wants.
Some Christians pray faithfully beside hospital beds and still walk into funeral homes.
Some marriages end despite years of tears and sincere attempts at reconciliation.
Some parents bury children.
Some people live with chronic pain.
Some prayers are answered in ways we would never have chosen.
John 11 is not a guarantee that every Christian will receive a Lazarus miracle in this life.
And anyone who uses this passage to promise that your loved one must be healed if you believe hard enough is promising more than Scripture promises.
Our hope is greater than that.
Because the ultimate Christian promise is not that we will never stand beside a grave.
It is that everyone who belongs to Christ will share in His resurrection life.
Jesus says in John 6:40 that He will raise up believers at the last day.
Revelation 21:4 promises a coming day when God will wipe away every tear and death will be no more.
Do you see the beauty?
At Lazarus' tomb, Jesus wept.
In the new creation, God will wipe away the tears of His people.
The story moves from a grieving Savior standing before a grave to the final defeat of everything that makes graves necessary.
And between those two realities, we live by faith.
Sometimes with trembling hands.
Sometimes with unanswered questions.
Sometimes with tears running down our faces while we whisper, "Lord, I still believe."
That is not a perfect, polished faith.
But faith does not need to be polished to cling to a perfect Savior.
Maybe that is you today.
Maybe you are not the person who needs another dramatic religious performance.
Maybe you need to stop pretending.
Maybe you need to admit that you are exhausted.
Maybe you need to confess the sin you have been protecting.
Maybe you need to forgive someone.
Maybe you need to seek help.
Maybe you need to return to prayer after months of spiritual silence.
Maybe you need to open your Bible again, not to create content or impress anyone, but because your soul is hungry.
Or maybe you simply need to know that the Jesus who stood outside Lazarus' tomb is not indifferent to human sorrow.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our High Priest is not unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.
He understands human suffering.
He knows what it means to be rejected, betrayed, misunderstood, and grieved.
And because He is the risen Lord, His compassion is joined to the power to save.
So bring Him the truth.
Not the edited version of your life.
Not the testimony you think other Christians want to hear.
The truth.
"Jesus, I am hurting."
"Jesus, I have sinned."
"Jesus, I am afraid."
"Jesus, I have been pretending."
"Jesus, I want to believe, but I am struggling."
You do not need to hide your tears from the Savior who shed His own.
And you do not need to hide your sins from the Savior who died to save sinners.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because He is merciful.
And if this message has exposed something you have been carrying in silence, I want to invite you to do something simple.
You do not have to explain everything publicly. God knows what is behind those words.
Someone else may need to hear that faith can survive sorrow.
There is also someone in your life who needs this message.
Someone who stopped attending church after a funeral.
Someone who believes God abandoned them when their prayers were not answered.
Someone who has been smiling in photographs while privately falling apart.
Someone who thinks their tears make them a bad Christian.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because the truth of God's Word deserves to travel farther than our immediate circles.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, forgiveness, and faithful discipleship.
That is also why I want to speak openly about something important.
Creating and sharing Gospel-centered resources takes time, effort, and financial support.
For Christians who choose to support Gospel ministry through their giving, that support can be an expression of generosity and stewardship.
But I want to be careful with something sacred.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not driven by guilt or pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Tithes and offerings are matters of Christian stewardship, and believers should seek to honor God faithfully in their giving, including their commitments to their local congregations.
Your worship belongs to Christ.
Your salvation rests in Christ.
These items are simply additional expressions of appreciation. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
The greater purpose is to keep making biblical truth accessible, understandable, and personally meaningful.
You can begin learning, reading, and growing without purchasing anything.
We are not building a community around a personality.
We want to build a community that keeps returning to the person and work of Jesus Christ.
Because one day, our books will wear out.
Our social media posts will be forgotten.
Our platforms will change.
Our possessions will pass away.
But the Word of the Lord endures forever.
And the Savior who wept outside Lazarus' tomb will remain the resurrection and the life.
Picture the stone.
The darkness.
The grieving sisters.
The people who had come to mourn.
And Jesus standing there, knowing exactly what He was about to do.
His eyes fill with tears.
He approaches the tomb.
The stone is removed.
And the voice that will one day summon the dead in the final resurrection calls out to Lazarus.
A dead man comes walking into the light.
But the deepest wonder of that day was not simply that Lazarus lived again.
It was that the One who held authority over death loved people deeply enough to stand with them in their sorrow.
That is the Jesus of Scripture.
Not an indifferent ruler who watches human suffering from a distance.
Not a powerless teacher who can only offer comforting words.
But the incarnate Son of God.
Full of grace and truth.
Compassionate toward the broken.
Holy in all His ways.
Mighty to save.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
And coming again.
So if you are standing beside something that feels like a tomb today, do not build your faith on a prediction about what God must do next.
Build it on the One who has already conquered death.
Trust His character when you cannot understand His timing.
Bring Him your grief without pretending.
Confess your sin without hiding.
Receive His grace through faith.
And remember that even when the answer is not the miracle you begged for, the resurrection of Jesus Christ remains the unshakable foundation of Christian hope.
The tears of Jesus at Lazarus' tomb remind us that the Savior who knows the end of the story still cares about the pain we experience before we reach it.
And perhaps that is what your weary heart has needed to hear all along.
The One who knew the grave would open still wept beside it—and the One who sees your tears has already walked out of His own.
